newsitem.title: ITALY: IMF concentrates minds on Italian welfare bill.
newsitem.headline: IMF concentrates minds on Italian welfare bill.

text.p: As Italy struggles desperately to qualify for a European currency union, concern is growing that efforts to clean up state finances could unravel unless the government takes an axe to welfare spending, economists said.

The International Monetary Fund was quoted at the weekend as saying that in its effort to qualify at all costs for EMU membership from the outset, Italy was neglecting to make badly needed "structural reforms" -- a code word for welfare cuts.
Italy is in a race against time to wrestle down the ratio of its public deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) to three percent by the end of the year in order to meet an EU deadline.

The IMF's warning came as a reminder that while Italy is doing everything to squeeze the last drop of revenue out of taxpayers with one-off measures, core components of state spending have been left largely unscathed.
"It's another drop of poison in Italy's teacup," said Sharda Persaud, an economist with San Paolo in London, referring to the IMF leak.

IMF documents leaked on Saturday came after a week in which financial markets were unnerved by reports -- subsequently denied -- that France and Germany were plotting to keep Italy out of the launch of a currency union.

"The watchword is sustainability. The underlying message from Germany is that the 1997 targets are not the be all and end all even if Italy meets them," said Ken Wattret, an economist with Banque Paribas in London.

Economists predict that unless there is a renewed fiscal tightening -- or a cut in state spending -- in next year's budget the deficit will balloon out to at least four percent of GDP in 1998 even if it meets the three percent target this year.
Market concerns are also firmly focused on the fragility of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition, which nearly collapsed two weeks ago over sending Italian troops to Albania.
The government relies on votes from the Marxist-inspired Communist Refoundation party in the lower house of parliament where it does not have an overall majority.

Another sign of weakness came when a commission of the lower house of parliament voted on Friday against a proposed 1997 mini-budget even though the package is expected to clear parliament if it is put to a confidence vote.
The supplementary budget aims to reduce the 1997 budget deficit by 15.5 trillion lire ($9.1 billion) in the hope of keeping Italy on track to meet the three percent deficit target.

But with many market commentators firmly convinced that Germany is determined to keep Italy out of the first wave of EMU members, economists are focusing as never before on the longer term prospects for bringing Italian public finances to heel.
"The government is struggling to impose its will. The next big event is going to be the 1998 budget, but if the government has its hands tied the risk is for another weak package," said Wattret.
The IMF did not mince its words in spelling out what it saw as the top priorities on the government's agenda.

ANSA quoted executive director Thomas Bernes as saying that financial markets would react more favourably to "a solid programme carried out over a longer period of time than to a series of ambitious but debatable measures."
"Such as the supplementary budget which does not contain structural measures on welfare spending," he added.

These words were echoed by former Bank of Italy number three, Tommaso Padoa Schioppa, last week who said it was more important for Italy to get its house in order, even if it meant joining late, than to enter EMU on time but only half prepared.
